summary: The note examines why rural telecommunication outages happen and what they cost communities, citing incidents in many towns from September 2023 to January 2024. Causes include a lack of redundant infrastructure, extreme weather and aging equipment, while impacts reach businesses, property values, schools, healthcare and emergency response. It closes by urging infrastructure investment, service diversification such as satellite, supportive government policy and community continuity planning.
one_line: Rural telecom outages stem from missing redundancy, weather and aging infrastructure, harming economies, education, health and emergencies, and call for investment and resilience planning.
key_facts: Cedarville residents experienced a network blackout on November 4th.
Maplewood lost service on the evening of September 15th, leaving the community potentially in danger.
Oakridge's service provider experienced a fiber cut on October 22nd; rural areas often lack the backup providers that urban areas have.
A lightning storm near Greenfield on October 12th left communication lines dead for hours.
Businessman David Thompson estimates the day-long Pineview blackout on December 1st cost his online retail company thousands in lost sales.
Franklin Orchards outside of Rosewood was affected by the network failure on November 28th, showing the impact on the farming community and supply chains.
In Ashton, the October 5th outage disrupted internet-based learning, putting 14-year-old Emma Robertson at a disadvantage compared to city peers.
The Riverdale shutdown on September 20th left many without access to medical consultations.

During the Wildwood outage on November 18th, neither landlines nor cell towers worked; George Harris, who suffered a heart attack that evening, survived through fortune and timely local human intervention.
The Bakersfield outage on January 15th, 2024 showed issues persisted even after awareness was raised.
Local official Susan O'Malley said: "Preparedness goes hand in hand with resilience. We need industry commitments to infrastructure investment, and we need it yesterday."
After the Grandview blackout on November 30th, satellite phones were distributed to key community personnel as a temporary measure.
The note argues government should level the playing field for rural telecom investment, as it did with rural electrification.
Proposed continuity planning includes equipping local emergency services with tools that don't rely on the larger grid, readiness programs and local communication networks.
